opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest difference is that in 2009, if you wanted to build an autonomous car, the perception problem alone was a massive research undertaking. You had to hand-engineer a lot of the pipeline: detecting pedestrians, segmenting lanes, building maps, and every one of those components was brittle in its own way. Machine learning was a tool you'd use for individual pieces, but it wasn't something you could build the whole system around.

Today, we're starting from a very different place. We have foundation models, vision-language models trained on enormous amounts of internet data, that already understand a lot about the world. They know what a cup is, what it means to put something in a drawer, roughly how objects relate to each other. So when we build a robotic foundation model, we're not starting from scratch. We can take a model that has absorbed a huge amount of semantic and visual knowledge and teach it to connect that knowledge to physical action. That's a qualitatively different starting point.

The other thing is that we now understand much better how to scale learning systems. In 2009 nobody really knew that if you just collected more data and trained bigger models, you'd get these smooth, predictable improvements and emergent generalization. Now we have a fairly good playbook for that. The challenge in robotics is that the data doesn't already exist on the internet the way text does, so we have to collect it, but once we have it, we know what to do with it.

And I think there's a subtler point too. Driving is in some ways a very unforgiving domain. The tolerance for error is extremely low, and the long tail is brutal. A lot of robotic manipulation tasks, like folding laundry, cleaning a kitchen, or assembling boxes, are more forgiving. If the robot fumbles a shirt, it can try again. That means you can deploy systems that are imperfect, let them get real-world experience, and improve them through that experience. That flywheel, deploying, collecting data, getting better, is much easier to get started in many robotics settings than it was for self-driving cars.

So I don't want to overstate it, because there are still very hard problems, but I think we're starting much further along the curve than driving was in 2009, and the path from here to broadly useful robots could be considerably shorter than people might assume based on that history.

r001.rationale: The response calls the 2009 perception pipeline brittle, but does not say it could produce an impressive demonstration before failing to generalize.

r002.rationale: It contrasts hand-engineered 2009 perception with modern vision-language models that already understand visual and semantic concepts, and presents that knowledge as a better starting point for robotics.

r003.rationale: It says that scaling learning systems with more data and larger models produces improvements and emergent generalization, linking scalability to generalizability.

r004.rationale: It describes a better technological starting point, but does not clearly distinguish that from robotics being inherently easier; it also cites manipulation tasks as more forgiving.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that in 2009, if you wanted to build a self-driving car, you basically had to invent the machine learning along the way. The learning tools that existed were pretty weak. You could do some perception with hand-engineered features, and most of the stack was essentially classical: you'd localize against a map, you'd have a planner, you'd have a controller, and learning was this small component that maybe helped you detect pedestrians a little better. So the whole problem had to be decomposed by hand into pieces that engineers could reason about individually, and that decomposition is where a lot of the difficulty and brittleness came from.

In 2025, the situation is almost reversed. We have learning systems that are extremely good at exactly the parts that were hardest to engineer: understanding what's in a scene, understanding language, representing commonsense knowledge about objects and how people use them. Large pretrained models give you a starting point where the robot already "knows" a lot about the world before it has ever done anything physical. So the question for robotics isn't "how do we build perception from scratch," it's "how do we connect this huge reservoir of knowledge to actual motor behavior." That's a very different and, I'd argue, much more tractable starting point.

The other thing that's changed is the methodology. In the autonomous driving era, you'd collect data to evaluate a system that was mostly designed by hand. Now the data is the system. The recipe that worked for language and vision, large diverse datasets plus a general architecture plus scaling, is something we can apply to robots end to end, and we have good evidence that it transfers. So instead of each robot being a bespoke engineering project, you can think about a single model that learns across many robots, many tasks, many environments, and gets better the more it sees.

I'd also add a note of caution, because people sometimes take this too far. Robots still have the problem that the data doesn't just exist on the internet the way text does. You have to go out and get it, and physical interaction is slow and expensive. So the starting point is much better in terms of the tools, but the hard part has moved. In 2009 the hard part was building the brain. In 2025 the brain is mostly there, and the hard part is grounding it: getting the experience, closing the loop, and making the thing actually robust in the messy real world. That's a problem I'm much more optimistic about than the one the self-driving folks faced, but it's not a solved problem.

r001.rationale: It describes hand-engineered perception and brittleness, but does not say such a system can make an impressive demonstration and then fail to generalize.

r002.rationale: It says modern learning systems and pretrained models provide strong scene understanding and a broad starting point, and describes transfer across robots, tasks, and environments.

r003.rationale: It links scaling and broad data to transfer, but does not equate machine-learning scalability with generalizability.

r004.rationale: It says the tools provide a better starting point and that grounding remains difficult, but does not distinguish that advantage from robotics being inherently easier than autonomous driving.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is that we’re starting with models that already know a tremendous amount about the world. If you were building an autonomous driving system in 2009, you had to construct a lot of the machinery for perception, prediction, and decision-making specifically for that problem. Now you can start with a pretrained model that can recognize objects, interpret a scene, and understand what a person is asking it to do.

That doesn’t mean it knows how to control a robot. There’s a substantial gap between being able to describe how to pick up a cup and actually picking it up reliably. But you’re learning that capability on top of a much richer foundation. You don’t necessarily have to learn what a cup is from your robot’s experience at the same time that you’re learning how to grasp it.

The other difference is that we have a much better recipe for building general-purpose models. You can imagine training one system on experience from many different tasks, where learning one task helps it do another. That makes the starting point for robotics quite promising.

I would still be cautious about translating that into a timeline. Physical interaction brings its own problems: collecting experience is expensive, mistakes have consequences, and reliability matters enormously. The technology gives us a very different starting point, but it doesn’t eliminate the need to solve those problems.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts task-specific 2009 systems with pretrained models, but does not say an engineered perception system can impress in a demonstration and then fail to generalize.

r002.rationale: It attributes robotics’ stronger starting point to pretrained models that already recognize objects and interpret scenes, alongside a general-purpose training approach that transfers learning across tasks.

r003.rationale: The response discusses training across tasks but does not equate machine-learning scalability with generalizability.

r004.rationale: It says the better starting point does not remove physical-interaction problems, but does not clearly distinguish that advantage from robotics being inherently easier than autonomous driving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that we’re starting with models that already know a lot about the world. If you were building an autonomous driving system in 2009, you had to build much of the perception and decision-making machinery specifically for driving. You couldn’t take an existing model and expect it to recognize all sorts of objects, understand instructions, or bring useful prior knowledge to a new situation.

With robotics today, we have that starting point. Now, knowing what a cup is and being able to talk about picking it up is very different from actually controlling a robot to pick it up. So there’s still a substantial gap. But the problem becomes: how do we connect these capabilities to physical actions, and how do we get the experience needed to improve those actions?

That also changes the economics of collecting data. If you have to learn everything from scratch, you need an enormous amount of experience before the system does anything useful. If you can reuse knowledge across tasks, objects, and environments, then each bit of robot experience can potentially go much further. I think that gives robotics a very different starting point, although it doesn’t mean the remaining problems are easy.

r001.rationale: The response says older driving systems needed specialized machinery, but does not describe an impressive demonstration that fails to generalize.

r002.rationale: It credits robotics’ stronger starting point to models that recognize many objects, understand instructions, and reuse knowledge across tasks and environments.

r003.rationale: It says reused knowledge can make each bit of robot experience go further, but does not equate machine-learning scalability with generalizability.

r004.rationale: The response notes that robotics still has substantial, difficult problems, but does not distinguish its better starting point from being inherently easier than autonomous driving.
